procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court in S.C. No. 113 of 2009
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 15.03.2010 of the High Court of Madras in CRLA No. 17 of 2010, which affirmed the Ld. Trial Court's order in S.C. No. 113 of 2009 dated 04.12.2009
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Madras heard Criminal Appeals No. 17, 22 and 24 of 2010, titled Udayakumar & Ors. v. The State of Tamil Nadu, and affirmed the Trial Court's judgment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Udayakumar (A-2), the convict, filed a Criminal Appeal (No. 1741 of 2010) in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the judgments of both the Trial Court and the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution successfully established the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.

facts: The High Court acquitted the two principal conspirators (A-1 and A-3) but convicted the appellant (A-2) for murder.
The conviction of A-2 was based solely on the identification made by a single eyewitness, PW-1.
The testimony of the eyewitness (PW-1) was contradicted by the testimony of the Investigating Officer (IO).
There was no other material evidence linking A-2 to the crime, such as evidence of him being hired, a link to the murder weapon (a sickle), or any scientific evidence.
law: The standard of proof in a criminal case is guilt 'beyond a reasonable doubt', not a 'preponderance of probability'.
In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of evidence must be completely established and must conclusively point to the guilt of the accused.
A conviction can be based on the testimony of a single eyewitness only if that witness is 'wholly reliable'. If the witness is not wholly reliable, their testimony requires independent corroboration.
The benefit of any doubt must be given to the accused to avoid a miscarriage of justice.
application: The Court found it illogical to convict A-2 when the alleged main conspirators were acquitted on the very same evidence, especially after the High Court disbelieved the conspiracy theory.
The prosecution's entire case against A-2 rested on the uncorroborated testimony of the single eyewitness, PW-1.
The Court deemed PW-1's testimony unreliable because it was contradicted by another prosecution witness, the IO.
The complete lack of any other corroborating evidence meant that the chain of circumstances was not established.
Given the unreliable nature of the sole piece of evidence and the acquittal of the co-accused, the Court found that the prosecution's case did not meet the high standard of proof required.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. The conviction was based on the uncorroborated and contradicted testimony of a single eyewitness, which was insufficient to prove the case, leading to the acquittal of the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts in this case.

facts: The lower courts had concurrent findings of fact regarding the guilt of accused A-2.
The High Court acquitted the main conspirators (A-1 and A-3) after disbelieving the prosecution's conspiracy theory.
However, the High Court upheld the conviction of A-2 for murder based on the same set of evidence, relying solely on the identification by a single eyewitness (PW-1).
The Supreme Court found that the testimony of this single eyewitness was contradicted and his version was belied by the testimony of the Investigating Officer (IO).
law: The Supreme Court's standard practice is not to interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts.
An exception to this rule exists for "exceptional cases or where gross errors have been committed which overlook crying circumstances and well established principles of criminal jurisprudence."
application: The Court found that this case fell into the category of an exceptional case with gross errors.

The primary error was the logical contradiction in the High Court's judgment: it acquitted the principal conspirators based on the evidence but convicted the alleged hired killer (A-2) using that same evidence.
The Court reasoned that if the conspiracy theory was disbelieved, there was no basis to uphold A-2's conviction, as the prosecution's case was built around it.

Furthermore, the conviction rested on the testimony of a single eyewitness which the Court found to be unreliable and contradicted, meaning the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the lower court's findings contained gross errors and contradictions, creating an exceptional circumstance that made it the Court's "bounden duty to correct such findings." Therefore, it decided to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction could be upheld after the High Court had disbelieved the theory of conspiracy.

facts: The prosecution's case was that A-1 and A-3 conspired to murder a victim and hired A-2 to carry out the killing.
The High Court disbelieved the prosecution's theory of conspiracy and acquitted the alleged main conspirators, A-1 and A-3.
Despite acquitting A-1 and A-3, the High Court upheld the murder conviction for A-2.
The conviction of A-2 was based on the same set of evidence that the High Court used to acquit the other co-accused.
law: The standard of proof in a criminal case is "beyond a reasonable doubt," not a mere "preponderance of probability."
To avoid a miscarriage of justice, the benefit of any doubt must be given to the accused.
It is illogical and contradictory to convict one accused while acquitting the principal conspirators on the very same set of evidence.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that once the High Court disbelieved the conspiracy theory, the entire foundation of the prosecution's case against A-2 collapsed.
The Court found it baseless to uphold A-2's conviction when the alleged principal conspirators (A-1 and A-3) had been acquitted based on the same evidence.
The Court noted that with the conspiracy theory gone, there was no other material on record to link A-2 to the crime or prove that he had been hired to commit the murder.
The Court criticized the High Court's judgment for lacking proper reasoning and for dealing with A-2's guilt in a "casual" manner.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction, holding that there was no basis to uphold it after the High Court had disbelieved the conspiracy theory. Since the main conspirators were acquitted on the same evidence, the prosecution had failed to prove A-2's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution successfully established the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution successfully established the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, justifying the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts in this case.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts as they were perverse and resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts, as they were well-reasoned.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction could be upheld after the High Court had disbelieved the theory of conspiracy.
appellant_arguments: The conviction could not be upheld because the prosecution's case collapsed once the theory of conspiracy was disbelieved by the High Court.
respondent_arguments: The conviction could be upheld based on other evidence on record, even without the conspiracy charge.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will only interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts in exceptional cases or where gross errors have been committed which overlook critical circumstances and well-established principles of criminal jurisprudence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. Once the High Court disbelieved the theory of conspiracy, there was no basis or reason to uphold the conviction, especially since the impugned judgment contained neither any reasoning nor any appreciation of the evidence on record. The concurrent findings of the lower courts contained gross errors, which made it the Supreme Court's bounden duty to interfere and correct the findings to avoid a miscarriage of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The prosecution must establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.

The Supreme Court interferes with concurrent findings of fact by the Courts below only in exceptional cases or where gross errors have been committed which overlook crying circumstances and well established principles of criminal jurisprudence.
A conviction cannot be based on the principles of preponderance of probability.
policy_considerations: It is our duty to make sure that miscarriage of justice is avoided at all costs and the benefit of doubt, if any, given to the accused.
In the attending circumstances, it becomes our bounden duty to correct such findings [of the lower courts].
